content:
Unit 2 opens. Mind mapping here is Tony Buzan's method specifically, not a generic bubble diagram — the laws are what make it work, and students will break most of them on their first attempt by design.

CORE IDEA
A list hides relationships. A Buzan map shows them — and the laws are what make the difference between a map and a doodle.

1. Radiant thinking. The brain does not store in lines; it radiates from a centre. A map on paper copies that shape, which is why recall improves.
2. The laws of emphasis. A central *image*, not a word. Three colours minimum in that image. Branch thickness heaviest at the centre and thinning outward. Varying letter size.
3. The laws of clarity. ONE key word per line. Print, do not join up. The word sits *on* the line. Line length equals word length. Curved branches, never straight rulered ones. Paper landscape.
4. Basic Ordering Ideas. The main branches off the centre are your BOIs — the four to seven big buckets. Get those right and the rest of the map organises itself.

active_learning_components.desc: What idea did you commit to in Session 5? What were the three questions you scored it against?
active_learning_components.rationale: Recall from memory, log closed, before any new input. Retrieval beats re-reading for retention.

active_learning_components.type: Warm-up: Map Your Morning — With No Rules
active_learning_components.desc: Students produce a lopsided list-with-boxes. When Buzan's laws land ten minutes later, they can see exactly which ones they broke and why it hurt the map.

active_learning_components.type: Check your morning map against the laws
active_learning_components.desc: Hold up your warm-up map. How many laws did it break? Almost everyone writes sentences, uses straight lines, and starts with a word instead of an image. Nobody is in trouble — that is the point of the exercise.

A3, landscape. Central IMAGE of the business — draw it, do not write the name. Three colours in that image. Four to seven BOIs as curved main branches, one key word each, printed on the line. Then radiate.
Second map, fresh sheet. The second map is always better because the BOIs are now obvious. Keep both.
3 minutes, individual. Hold the second map up during beat 4 and point at one branch — do not read the map aloud.
Which BOI did your second map have that your first did not?

early_finisher_extension: Redraw your second map with a different central image. Does the branch structure hold?
worked_example: Build one on the board while they watch. A chai stall. Draw a glass in the middle — badly — and say why it is a picture and not a word. Curve the first branch and say why it is not ruled. Write one word on it and say why not three. Two minutes, narrating each law as you apply it. This is the single most important two minutes of Unit 2: students copy what they saw done, not what they were told.
between_sessions: None. Bring both maps to Session 7.
